description: Deduct-value curve data for asphalt concrete pavements. The distress curves are first-pass anchor points read off the published figures in the supplied standard; they are PROVISIONAL because that read has not been verified. The X3.26 correction curves are still placeholder fits.

source.document: ASTM D 6433-99, Standard Practice for Roads and Parking Lots Pavement Condition Index Surveys
source.extraction_method: manual first-pass read of the raster figures

cdv_figure_note: The AC corrected-deduct-value curve is Fig. X3.26. The standard's own cross-reference at 9.5.5.3 says 'Fig. X4.15 in Appendix X3', but X4.15 is Railroad Crossing in the PCC appendix; the cross-reference is wrong in the 1999 edition. Fig. X3.26 is the AC corrected-deduct-value curve. These are still the MDPI placeholder fits and are the weakest numbers in this dataset: the vendored x3_26_cdv_validation_points.csv shows them reading 3 to 66 points high, and 100 where the standard's example says 58.

distress_curves.note: Anchor points read off Fig. X3.1 of the supplied ASTM D6433-99 raster scan, status UNVERIFIED_FIRST_PASS_DIGITIZATION. They are a read of the published graph rather than a fit to it, so they are usable, but three to four points per curve is coarse: a detection between anchors is interpolated, not measured. Confirm against the figure. The density axis is treated as logarithmic, which the standard's figures are drawn on. The vendored package asks for this to be validated first, and it has not been, so the exposure is measured rather than assumed: reading these same anchors on a linear axis instead changes the deduct value by up to 14.8 points, and PCI moves one-for-one with CDV. The evidence for the axis is in the anchors themselves -- 255 of 284 sit exactly on a power of ten, which a linear grid would not produce.
